citeAs: Welbl, Johannes, Nelson F. Liu, and Matt Gardner. (2017). Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions.
creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
description: SciQ is a dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions created via a two-step crowdsourcing process using science study textbooks and model-assisted distractor suggestions. The paper also describes a direct-answer version with associated passages, though it is slightly smaller because some passages come from unreleasable texts.
name: SciQ
rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk with Master's status; a total of 175 workers participated in the whole crowdsourcing project.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality analysis included reporting that 92.8% of questions passed validation in the second task, that workers accepted model-suggested distractors around half of the time, and a qualitative evaluation where people identified the original science exam question over a crowdsourced one in 55% of cases, below significance under a random-guess null hypothesis.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset was created in two crowdsourcing tasks. In the first, workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one or rejected all, and wrote a science exam question answerable from the passage, following instructions such as no yes/no questions, no ambiguity, question length 6-30 words, and answer length up to 3 words. In the second, another worker validated whether the question could appear in a school science exam, selected up to two model-suggested distractors, and wrote at least one additional distractor so there were three total.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly notes that having workers conceive original questions from scratch repeatedly risks falling into specific lexical and structural patterns. To reduce this, the authors used textbook passages to enforce diversity in question content and lexical expression, let workers choose among three candidate paragraphs, and shifted the task from pure generation to selection, modification, and validation.
rai:dataCollection: The authors compiled a base corpus of 28 science study books from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax, filtered paragraphs with a rule-based document filter, then crowdsourced question generation and distractor creation in two steps on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers first generated question-answer pairs from selected textbook paragraphs, then other workers validated questions and finalized distractors using model suggestions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data consisted of science study textbooks from 28 books covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax. Individual paragraphs from these books served as the passages used to formulate questions.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that the direct-answer version is slightly smaller because a small percentage of passages came from unreleasable texts. It also notes that model-suggested distractors were not reliable enough to use without human filtering, and that generating high-quality multiple-choice science questions is difficult because poor distractors can make questions trivial.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors randomly shuffled the collected dataset and split it into training, validation, and test portions, with 1,000 questions each in validation and test and the remainder in training. They also created a direct-answer version by pairing questions with associated passages and excluding some examples with unreleasable texts.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Before crowdsourcing, the authors applied a rule-based document filter to individual textbook paragraphs. Sentences were filtered out based on lexical, grammatical, pragmatic, and complexity rules, including removing questions or exclamations, sentences without a verb phrase, those with modal verbs or imperative phrases, certain pronouns, first names, very short or very long sentences, special characters, references to graphs/tables/web links, discourse markers, absolute wording, and instructional vocabulary; a paragraph was accepted if a minimum number of sentences was accepted.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for research on multiple choice science question answering, direct-answer reading comprehension with associated passages, studying neural model performance in medium-sized data settings, and augmenting training data for answering real 4th- and 8th-grade science exam questions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: A noisy classifier was used to find relevant passages, a rule-based document filter screened textbook paragraphs, and a random-forest distractor ranking model suggested plausible distractors to crowd workers.
